## Introduction and overview {#intro}

  -------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Module               Deep Learning for Image Restoration and Synthesis
  Official title       Apprentissage Profond pour la Restauration et la Synthese d’Images
  Instructors          A. ALMANSA, S. LADJAL, A. NEWSON (master-mva.com, 2026–2027)
  Period               Semester 2 · period 2 (04/01/2027 – 02/04/2027)
  Credits and volume   5 ECTS · 36 h (lectures 24 h, labs 12 h) per the Université Paris-Saclay programme table
  Label                [Learning]{.badge .label} · domains on master-mva.com: Image processing
  Language             English or French, according to the preferences of the audience (master-mva.com)
  Assessment           Individual lab reports, and an individual project with a report and an oral defence at the end of the course (master-mva.com); “partial continuous assessment” (Université Paris-Saclay); no weights displayed
  Prerequisites        Applied mathematics (linear algebra, numerical analysis, differential calculus, Fourier analysis) and programming (Python, Matlab); basic notions of image processing, optimisation and deep learning are useful but are introduced in the course (master-mva.com)
  -------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Audience**: a student with a good M1 in mathematics, computer science or physics who has met convolution and gradient descent, and wants to understand when a neural network really improves an image and when it only seems to.

**Empirical first**: a network trained to super-resolve images that were downsampled with the bicubic kernel looks excellent on its benchmark, then produces ringing and hallucinated textures on a real camera image, whose blur is different. A denoiser trained with the squared loss returns images that are visibly too smooth, even though its PSNR is the best available.

This course studies image models: the assumptions on natural images that turn an ill-posed restoration problem into a solvable one, and that let a machine synthesise new images. Deep learning is presented as the latest of these models, side by side with the variational and statistical models that preceded it, on denoising, deblurring, super-resolution, texture synthesis and image generation. It builds on [Deep Learning](../s1-deep-learning/index.html), [Image Denoising: the Human–Machine Competition](../s1-image-denoising/index.html) and [Convex Optimization and Applications in Machine Learning](../s1-convex-optimization/index.html), and it runs alongside [Generative Models for Images](../s2-generative-models-images/index.html) and [Inverse Problems and Imaging](../s2-inverse-problems-imaging/index.html).

### What you will be able to do

-   Write a restoration task (denoising, deblurring, super-resolution, inpainting) as a forward model and diagnose its ill-posedness in the Fourier domain.
-   Derive the Wiener filter, the Tikhonov and total-variation estimators, and wavelet shrinkage, and say which image model each one encodes.
-   Train a convolutional denoiser or super-resolution network, choose its loss, and predict what that loss does to the output (posterior mean, median, blur).
-   Prove that training on pairs of noisy images (Noise2Noise) has the same minimiser as training on clean targets.
-   Solve a linear inverse problem with plug-and-play ADMM, prove its fixed-point convergence under the bounded-denoiser assumption, and relate a denoiser to the score through Tweedie's formula.
-   Synthesise textures with random phase noise, with Gram-matrix statistics of a convolutional network, and with a spectrum constraint.
-   Derive the evidence lower bound, implement a variational autoencoder, and explain why its samples are blurry.
-   Derive the optimal discriminator of a GAN, relate the GAN game to the Jensen–Shannon and Wasserstein distances, and train a WGAN-GP.
-   State and prove the perception–distortion trade-off, and evaluate a restoration method with distortion and perceptual metrics without falling into their classical traps.
-   Sample from a posterior with a diffusion model or with Langevin dynamics driven by a denoiser, and say what can go wrong.

### Official objectives and syllabus (2026–2027)

The course description on master-mva.com starts from an observation: smaller sensors and larger computing power have made images ubiquitous, but those images need more and more demanding post-processing (filtering, restoration) to reach good quality. At the heart of such processing lie image models, which make efficient algorithms possible, and deep learning is the most recent of a long list of them.

The stated goal is to put recent deep-learning techniques for image quality in perspective with the methods that existed before them. The course explores denoising, super-resolution, deblurring, texture synthesis and the generation of natural images, presents the strengths and limitations of each technique, and analyses the methods critically, sometimes showing the pitfalls into which they fell.

The description lists five themes, each made of a lecture and a lab, and announces 8 sessions of 3 h (lecture and lab), 2 revision sessions and 1 project-presentation session, on Tuesday afternoons at Télécom Paris. The Université Paris-Saclay programme table gives 24 h of lectures and 12 h of labs, under partial continuous assessment. Every item is matched below.

| Official topic | Course section |
|---|---|
| 1\. End-to-end deep learning and application to super-resolution (S. Ladjal, 1 lecture + 1 lab) | [ch. 2](#ch2): supervised restoration, losses, DnCNN, Noise2Noise, SRCNN, sub-pixel convolution, pitfalls; sessions 3–4 |
| 2\. Inverse problems, variational, statistical and hybrid methods (A. Almansa, 1 lecture + 1 lab) | [ch. 1](#ch1) (variational and statistical models) and [ch. 3](#ch3) (MAP and MMSE, ADMM, plug-and-play, Tweedie, RED, unrolled networks); sessions 2, 5–6 |
| 3\. Generative models for texture synthesis (S. Ladjal, 1 lecture + lab) | [ch. 4](#ch4): random phase noise, Gram matrices (Gatys et al.), spectrum constraint (Liu et al.), feed-forward networks, style transfer; session 7 |

Extensions beyond the syllabus: Noise2Noise and the degradation-mismatch pitfall (ch. 2), the perception–distortion trade-off (ch. 7), diffusion models and Langevin posterior sampling (ch. 8), and a self-study chapter of research directions (ch. 9).

### Where this course fits in the programme

Official prerequisites (master-mva.com): applied mathematics (linear algebra, numerical analysis, differential calculus, Fourier analysis) and programming (Python, Matlab). Basic notions of image processing, optimisation and deep learning are useful, but the course introduces them; ch. 0 reviews what is needed.

-   **Refreshers** — [Linear Algebra, Analysis and Optimization](../s0-refresher-linear-algebra-optimization/index.html) (SVD, gradients, convexity), [Probability and Statistics](../s0-refresher-probability-statistics/index.html) (conditional expectation, Gaussian vectors, Bayes), [Scientific Python, NumPy and PyTorch](../s0-refresher-python-scientific-computing/index.html) (every lab).
-   **First-semester courses that prepare it** — [Deep Learning](../s1-deep-learning/index.html), [Image Denoising: the Human–Machine Competition](../s1-image-denoising/index.html), [Convex Optimization](../s1-convex-optimization/index.html) (proximal operators, ADMM), [Introduction to Probabilistic Graphical Models and Deep Generative Models](../s1-probabilistic-graphical-models/index.html) (variational inference), [Sub-Pixel Image Processing](../s1-sub-pixel-image-processing/index.html) (sampling, aliasing), [Computational Statistics](../s1-computational-statistics/index.html) (Langevin, MCMC), [Optimal Transport for Machine Learning](../s1-optimal-transport-ml/index.html) (Wasserstein distance), [Stochastic Calculus in Machine Learning](../s1-stochastic-calculus-ml/index.html) (diffusion processes).
-   **Related second-semester courses** — [Generative Models for Images](../s2-generative-models-images/index.html), [Inverse Problems and Imaging](../s2-inverse-problems-imaging/index.html), [Diffusion and Multiscale Models in Artificial Intelligence](../s2-diffusion-multiscale/index.html), [Deep Learning in Practice](../s2-deep-learning-in-practice/index.html), [Deep Learning for Medical Imaging](../s2-deep-learning-medical-imaging/index.html), [Bayesian Machine Learning](../s2-bayesian-ml/index.html), [Remote Sensing Data](../s2-remote-sensing/index.html).
-   **Afterwards** — the [Research Internship](../s3-research-internship/index.html): restoration and generative modelling are frequent internship subjects in imaging laboratories and companies.

### Course outline

-   **Review: images, Fourier analysis, estimation and network training** — the discrete Fourier transform, the convolution theorem, aliasing, the MMSE and MAP estimators, and convolutional layers.
-   **Image degradations and classical image models** — forward models, quality metrics, Wiener, Tikhonov, total variation, wavelet shrinkage and patch models.
-   **End-to-end deep learning for denoising and super-resolution** — supervised restoration, what the loss estimates, DnCNN, Noise2Noise, SRCNN, sub-pixel convolution and the pitfalls of synthetic training data.
-   **Inverse problems: variational, statistical and hybrid methods** — MAP and MMSE, proximal splitting, plug-and-play ADMM and its convergence, Tweedie's formula, RED and unrolled networks.
-   **Generative models for texture synthesis** — random phase noise, Gram matrices of convolutional features, the spectrum constraint and feed-forward texture networks.
-   **Autoencoders and variational autoencoders** — linear autoencoders and PCA, the evidence lower bound, the reparameterisation trick and the limits of VAEs.
-   **Generative adversarial networks** — the minimax game, the Jensen–Shannon and Wasserstein distances, conditional GANs for restoration and the evaluation of generators.
-   **Perception, distortion and the critical evaluation of restoration** — why no estimator can be both accurate and realistic, and how metrics mislead.
-   **Diffusion models and generative priors for inverse problems** — denoising score matching, DDPM, and posterior sampling with Langevin dynamics and diffusion guidance.
-   **Research directions and open problems** — convergent plug-and-play, uncertainty, self-supervision, memorisation (self-study).

### Session plan {#sessions}

**36 h in class = 12 sessions of 3 h.** The volume is the official one of the Université Paris-Saclay programme table (24 h of lectures and 12 h of labs); master-mva.com organises the course as 8 sessions of 3 h (lecture and lab), 2 revision sessions and 1 project-presentation session, and the split below into 12 sessions is a proposal that follows the order of the five official themes.

Level 1 = foundations (reviews, definitions, first worked examples), 2 = core methods and their proofs, 3 = advanced material close to current research; the level never goes down from one session to the next. The two revision sessions are used for two cross-cutting chapters that revisit the earlier ones.

| Session | Hours | Level | Content | Practice |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 3 h | 1 | ch. 0 Review: DFT and convolution theorem, sampling and aliasing, MMSE and MAP, convolutional layers and training | Ex. 1, 2 |
| 2 | 3 h | 1 | ch. 1 Forward models, PSNR and SSIM, inverse filter, Wiener and Tikhonov, total variation, wavelet shrinkage, patch models | Ex. 3, 4; lab: deconvolution (code of ch. 1) |
| 3 | 3 h | 2 | ch. 2.1–2.3 Supervised restoration, what the L2 and L1 losses estimate, DnCNN and residual learning, Noise2Noise | Ex. 6; lab: train the denoiser of ch. 2 |
| 4 | 3 h | 2 | ch. 2.4–2.6 Super-resolution: SRCNN, sub-pixel convolution, perceptual losses, pitfalls of synthetic degradations | Ex. 5; lab: super-resolution (official theme 1) |
| 5 | 3 h | 2 | ch. 3.1–3.3 Bayesian inverse problems, MAP versus MMSE, proximal operators, ADMM, plug-and-play ADMM and its convergence | Ex. 7 |
| 6 | 3 h | 2 | ch. 3.4–3.5 Tweedie's formula, regularisation by denoising, unrolled networks | lab: plug-and-play deblurring (official theme 2) |
| 7 | 3 h | 2 | ch. 4 Texture synthesis: random phase noise, Gram matrices, spectrum constraint, feed-forward networks, style transfer | Ex. 8; lab: textures (official theme 3) |
| 8 | 3 h | 2 | ch. 5 Autoencoders and PCA, latent variable models, ELBO, reparameterisation, limitations of VAEs | Ex. 9, 11; lab: VAE (official theme 4) |
| 9 | 3 h | 3 | ch. 6.1–6.3 The GAN game, optimal discriminator, Jensen–Shannon, training pathologies, Wasserstein GAN | Ex. 10 |
| 10 | 3 h | 3 | ch. 6.4–6.5 Conditional GANs for restoration, evaluation (FID), adversarial mixture clustering | lab: GAN against WGAN-GP (official theme 5) |
| 11 | 3 h | 3 | ch. 7 Perception–distortion trade-off, posterior sampling, metrics and pitfalls (first revision session: revisits ch. 2, 4, 6) | Ex. 12, 13 |
| 12 | 3 h | 3 | ch. 8 Denoising score matching, DDPM, Langevin and diffusion posterior sampling (second revision session: revisits ch. 3, 5) | Ex. 14 |

**Self-study, outside the 36 h** (about 5 h in total): ch. 9 Research directions and open problems (≈ 3 h, with Ex. 15) · the code blocks of ch. 7–8 run and modified at home (≈ 2 h).

### How to study this module

-   Read ch. 0 before the first session even if you know the material: the convolution theorem, aliasing and the MMSE estimator are used in every later chapter without warning.
-   After each session, run the code block of the chapter, change one parameter (noise level, blur width, loss, regularisation weight) and predict the effect before looking.
-   Do the exercises listed in the *Practice* column right after the session; the ★ ones check the session, the ★★ ones prepare the next.
-   Keep a lab notebook: the official assessment includes individual lab reports, and the labs of sessions 2–10 are where they come from.
-   Read ch. 7 twice, once after ch. 2 and once after ch. 6: it is the critical lens the course description asks for.
-   Environment: Python 3 with NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn (its two bundled sample images and the digits data set) and PyTorch on CPU; every code block runs in well under a minute on a laptop.
